section.title: The Crucifixion and Burial
section.sectionRationale: The hour toward which the whole Gospel has moved arrives. Jesus is flogged, mocked as a king, and handed over to be crucified. On the cross He entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple and, having accomplished all, cries, It is finished, and yields up His spirit. John draws out the fulfillment of Scripture at every turn: the unbroken bones of the Passover lamb, the pierced side, the parted garments, and a burial by Joseph and Nicodemus in a garden tomb.
section.thesis: The King of the Jews reigns from a cross, bearing mockery and death in sovereign obedience, and having accomplished all the Father gave Him He declares it finished and lays down His life, His unbroken bones and pierced side marking Him as the true Passover Lamb whose death, foretold in Scripture, is complete and is sealed by an honorable burial.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the flogging, mockery, and Pilate's Here is the man; the sentence and the crucifixion with its inscription; the parted garments and the care for His mother; the accomplished work, It is finished, and the pierced side; and the burial in the garden tomb.

verses.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and had Him flogged.
The soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns, set it on His head, and dressed Him in a purple robe.
And they went up to Him again and again, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and slapping Him in the face.
Once again Pilate came out and said to the Jews, “Look, I am bringing Him out to you to let you know that I find no basis for a charge against Him.”
When Jesus came out wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!”
As soon as the chief priests and officers saw Him, they shouted, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” “You take Him and crucify Him,” Pilate replied, “for I find no basis for a charge against Him.”
“We have a law,” answered the Jews, “and according to that law He must die, because He declared Himself to be the Son of God.”
When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid,
and he went back into the Praetorium. “Where are You from?” he asked. But Jesus gave no answer.
So Pilate said to Him, “Do You refuse to speak to me? Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?”
Jesus answered, “You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin.”
From then on, Pilate tried to release Him, but the Jews kept shouting, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar.”
When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha.
It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. And Pilate said to the Jews, “Here is your {{basileus|King}}!”
At this, they shouted, “Away with Him! Away with Him! Crucify Him!” “Shall I crucify your King?” Pilate asked. “We have no king but Caesar,” replied the chief priests.
Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took Him away.
Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha.
There they crucified Him, and with Him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle.
Pilate also had a notice posted on the cross. It read: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Many of the Jews read this sign, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but only that He said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom.

So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did.
Near the cross of Jesus stood His mother and her sister, as well as Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene.
When Jesus saw His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing nearby, He said to His mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.

units.label: It is finished
units.note: the Lamb whose bones are not broken

verses.text: After this, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.”
A jar of sour wine was sitting there. So they soaked a sponge in the wine, put it on a stalk of {{hyssopos|hyssop}}, and lifted it to His mouth.
When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “{{teleo|It is finished}}.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.

It was the day of Preparation, and the next day was a High Sabbath. In order that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed.
So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man who had been crucified with Jesus, and those of the other.
But when they came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out.
The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.
Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not one of His bones will be broken.”
And, as another Scripture says: “They will look on the One they have pierced.”

units.label: The burial
units.note: a new tomb in a garden

verses.text: Afterward, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews), asked Pilate to let him remove the body of Jesus. Pilate gave him permission, so he came and removed His body.
Nicodemus, who had previously come to Jesus at night, also brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds.
So they took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, according to the Jewish burial custom.
Now there was a garden in the place where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.
And because it was the Jewish day of Preparation and the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there.

basileus.gloss: King. The title saturates the crucifixion: the soldiers mock Him as King of the Jews, Pilate presents Him as your King, and the charge posted on the cross in three languages proclaims Him King. John's irony is profound: the mockery states the truth. Jesus really is the King, reigning from the cross, and the world unknowingly proclaims His royalty even while crucifying Him.

hyssopos.gloss: Hyssop, the small plant used to daub the Passover lamb's blood on the doorframes in Exodus 12. John notes the sour wine was lifted on hyssop, a deliberate Passover echo. As Jesus dies at the time the Passover lambs are prepared, the detail marks Him as the true Passover Lamb whose blood shields His people from death.

teleo.gloss: To finish, complete, accomplish, bring to its intended goal. Jesus' cry, It is finished, is a single word in Greek, tetelestai, a shout of completion, not defeat. The word was used for paying a debt in full. The saving work the Father gave Him is done, the Scriptures fulfilled, the price paid; nothing remains to be added.

basic.context: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers crown Him with thorns and mock Him as king. Pilate keeps declaring Him innocent, yet, pressured by the threat that releasing a self-styled king makes him no friend of Caesar, he hands Jesus over. Jesus carries His cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, with a sign proclaiming Him King of the Jews in three languages. From the cross He entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple. Knowing all was accomplished, He cries, It is finished, and yields up His spirit. His bones are not broken and His side is pierced, fulfilling Scripture, and Joseph and Nicodemus bury Him in a new garden tomb.
basic.hermeneutics: John presents the cross as the throne and the hour of glory, not merely tragedy. The recurring title King and the trilingual sign proclaim Jesus' royalty even in mockery. The key words are It is finished, a cry of completion. Watch how John points repeatedly to fulfilled Scripture, the unbroken bones and pierced side marking Jesus as the Passover Lamb. The blood and water and the eyewitness testimony are given so that we may believe.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is saturated with kingship: Jesus is mocked and proclaimed basileus, King, and the truth shines through the irony. The hyssopos, hyssop, that lifts the wine recalls the Passover. And His final cry is a single Greek word, tetelestai, from teleo, it is finished, the shout that the saving work is complete.
basic.typology: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb: He dies as the lambs are prepared, His bones are not broken as the Passover lamb's must not be, and hyssop appears as at the first Passover. The pierced side fulfills Zechariah's prophecy. The garden tomb echoes the garden where the story of humanity began.
basic.christ: Christ reigns from the cross as King, the innocent Son of God condemned in the place of sinners. He is the Passover Lamb whose death shields His people, and He completes the saving work with the cry, It is finished, laying down His life in sovereign obedience.
basic.god: God is sovereign over the whole scene; even Pilate's authority is given from above. The Father's saving plan, foretold in Scripture, is accomplished exactly, so that the cross is no accident but the fulfillment of God's purpose to save.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 gives the Passover lamb and hyssop. Psalm 22 foretells the parted garments and thirst. Zechariah 12 foretells the pierced One. Isaiah 53 describes the servant's death and burial with the rich.
basic.oneStory: The King of the world reigns from a cross, the true Passover Lamb whose blood delivers His people. When He cries, It is finished, the saving work promised since the fall is complete; the Scriptures are fulfilled to the last detail, and He is laid in a garden tomb, ready for the dawn of new creation.

context.literary:
John 19 is the second half of the Roman trial that began at 18:28 and the Gospel's account of the hour toward which everything has leaned since 2:4. It is arranged in two large panels. In the first, verses 1 to 16, Pilate moves between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside, and the last three scenes press the question of who really holds authority: the mockery and 'Here is the man,' verses 1 to 8, the exchange about where Jesus is from and where authority comes from, verses 9 to 11, and the final sentence under the pressure of the words 'no friend of Caesar,' verses 12 to 16. In the second panel, verses 17 to 42, the scene moves to the place of the skull and is built around a series of small units tied together by the word fulfil. Each of the four soldiers' acts and the three last sayings of Jesus carries a note that Scripture is being completed, verses 24, 28, 36 and 37.

The centre of the chapter is the sign over the cross and the title it carries. Every phase of the story uses the language of kingship: the mockery of 'Hail, King of the Jews,' verse 3, Pilate's 'Here is your King,' verse 14, the priests' confession 'We have no king but Caesar,' verse 15, and the sign posted on the cross, verse 19. John makes the mockers speak the truth without knowing it. The irony reaches its height when the chief priests, the guardians of Israel's covenant, say they have no king but Caesar, which is the opposite of the confession of Israel's faith.

The pace changes again after Jesus dies. Verses 28 to 30 are slow, with the word 'accomplished' used twice, and verses 31 to 37 are marked by one eyewitness, who stresses that his testimony is true so that readers may believe, verse 35. Then Joseph and Nicodemus appear, two men who had been secret, and they do in public what the Twelve could not. The chapter closes on a garden and a new tomb, verses 41 and 42, setting up the morning of chapter 20.
context.historical:
Roman flogging was a savage preliminary to crucifixion, using a whip with pieces of bone or metal, and it often killed or crippled. John mentions it in a line, verse 1, because he is interested less in the physical horror than in who is being tortured. The soldiers' mockery in verses 2 and 3 is a parody of a coronation. A crown, a royal purple robe and a salute modelled on the greeting to the emperor are given to someone they think is a laughable pretender. For people who knew that provincial rebels were regularly executed as pretenders to a throne, it would have been recognizable and cruel.

Pilate's problem is political. The Jewish leaders move from the charge of blasphemy, 'He declared Himself to be the Son of God,' verse 7, which cites the law against blasphemy in Leviticus 24:16, to a political charge that a Roman governor cannot ignore: 'If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar,' verse 12. A governor who let a claimant to kingship go free could be reported to the emperor, and Pilate's tenure in Judea was not secure. The scene turns on that fear. The judgment seat is set on the Stone Pavement, called Gabbatha in Aramaic, verse 13, and it is the Day of Preparation, the day before the weekly Sabbath and the beginning of the feast.

Crucifixion was done outside the city walls, and a notice, a titulus, was normally displayed to tell the crime. The sign was in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, the languages of religion, government and common speech, so that all could read it, verse 20. The soldiers divided the clothes of the condemned as a matter of course. Under the law of Moses a body hung on a tree could not stay overnight, Deuteronomy 21:23, and with a High Sabbath at hand the leaders asked for the legs to be broken to hasten death, verse 31. Breaking the legs made it impossible to push up to breathe. When the soldiers found Jesus already dead, they did not break His legs, but one pierced His side.

The burial is of high rank. Seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, verse 39, is an extravagant quantity, in the manner of a royal funeral. The Old Testament mentions a king laid on a bier full of spices, 2 Chronicles 16:14. And the tomb was new, in a garden, verses 41 and 42, belonging to a rich man, a detail that fits Isaiah's words that the Servant would be with a rich man in His death, Isaiah 53:9.
context.canonical:
The chapter's three explicit citations come from three different parts of the Old Testament, and together they claim that the whole Bible converges on this scene. The division of garments and casting of lots is from Psalm 22:18, a psalm of a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies, whose opening cry Jesus has already made His own in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34. The thirst, verse 28, is related to Psalm 69:21, 'they gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.' The unbroken bones come from the Passover regulations in Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12, and also from Psalm 34:20, which says of the righteous that 'He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken.' And the looking on the pierced one is from Zechariah 12:10, where the LORD says 'they will look on Me, the One they have pierced.'

The New Testament develops each of these. Paul writes 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. Peter says believers were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. John the Baptist's first greeting, 'Look, the Lamb of God,' 1:29, finds its answer here. The pierced one of Zechariah returns in Revelation 1:7, where every eye will see Him, even those who pierced Him. Zechariah 13:1 then promises a fountain opened to cleanse from sin and impurity, and many readers hear it behind the blood and water.

The cross is also the place where curse and blessing are exchanged. Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, and Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. Hebrews says Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify the people by His own blood, Hebrews 13:12. Colossians 2:14 sees the debt that stood against us nailed to the cross. The two last items, that He was buried and rose on the third day, are held together in Paul's earliest summary, 1 Corinthians 15:3 and 4. John's burial account is the first part of that pair, and the garden tomb prepares for the second.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John tells the story of the cross as the enthronement of the king. The way he organizes the details makes this plain. Every humiliation is set in the language of a coronation, a throne, a title and a procession, and the narrator never lets the reader forget who is being treated this way. His purpose is to turn what looked like defeat into the revelation of glory, and to do it without softening the shame. He includes the flogging, the thorns, the nails, the spear and the burial, because the glory is in the shame.

He also wants his readers to see that the cross was the plan. The citations of Scripture in verses 24, 28, 36 and 37 are not decoration. They show that each detail, down to the soldiers' division of the clothing, falls within what God had said beforehand. Jesus, knowing that 'everything had now been accomplished,' verse 28, speaks the single word that gives the thirst its meaning, and then declares the work finished. The cross is therefore not a tragedy God salvaged but the completion of a work the Father gave Him.

And John wants a response. He steps out of the story at verse 35 to say that the eyewitness has told what he saw so that 'you also may believe.' This is the aim the Gospel states in 20:31. The reader is invited to stand where the beloved disciple stood and to look on the one who was pierced. The burial of Jesus by Joseph and Nicodemus adds a second invitation. Those who had been afraid come into the open, and the reader is asked whether to do the same.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what people did to Jesus and what He did on the cross, and nearly all of it is without any command attached. The soldiers' cruelty, Pilate's weakness, the priests' denial of their own king and the disciples' absence are recorded as they happened, and none is a pattern to copy. What belongs to application is the way John presents the response of the few who are faithful. The mother, the beloved disciple and the other women stand by the cross when most have fled. Joseph and Nicodemus come forward at the cost of their standing. Jesus' words to His mother and the disciple, 'Woman, here is your son,' 'Here is your mother,' verses 26 and 27, show Him caring for His family in the middle of His agony. John records that the disciple took her into his home 'from that hour,' and the church has seen in that an example of the household of faith caring for its own, though the passage reports a specific act and does not lay down a rule.

The statement 'It is finished' is a declaration and not an instruction, and it tells us the work of atonement is complete. Believers do not add to it, and this is the ground on which Paul says that we have been justified, Romans 5:1. What believers are told to do in light of it comes in other texts: to follow the Lamb, to carry the cross after Him as a pattern of costly obedience, and to look to the one who was pierced in repentance and faith.

debates.question: How do John's 'sixth hour' and Mark's 'third hour' fit together?

views.label: John uses Roman civil time
views.case: If John counted from midnight, as the Romans did for civil purposes, the sixth hour of verse 14 is about six in the morning, and the trial ends before the third hour by Jewish reckoning, about nine, when Mark says they crucified Him, Mark 15:25. This was proposed by some early readers and is still held by some.

views.label: The hours are approximate
views.case: Ancient people measured the day roughly, in blocks of three hours. 'About the sixth hour,' as John words it in verse 14, is a loose marker for late morning, and Mark's 'third hour' for the start of the process. The two do not need to agree to the minute.

views.label: Different events are in view
views.case: John's hour marks the end of the trial and the sentence. Mark's marks the crucifixion itself, and the interval between them includes the carrying of the cross and the preparations. In this view the two accounts describe different moments.

debates.bearing: The point for John is the day, the Preparation for the Passover, not the clock. Whatever the hour, Pilate says 'Here is your King' at the time the Passover lambs were being made ready.

debates.question: What is the meaning of the blood and water in verse 34?

views.label: A physical sign of real death
views.case: John stresses that the flow was observed and that his testimony is true, verse 35. On this reading it is evidence that Jesus was truly dead and truly human, against any claim that He only seemed to suffer, a concern that appears in 1 John 5:6, 'not by water alone, but by water and blood.'

views.label: A sign of cleansing and new life
views.case: Blood speaks of the sacrifice that cleanses, and water of the Spirit given to renew. John 7:38 and 39 spoke of rivers of living water flowing from the one who is glorified, and that was to be the Spirit. The fountain opened for cleansing in Zechariah 13:1 stands in the background for many interpreters.

views.label: A picture of the sacraments
views.case: Many in church history have seen the water as baptism and the blood as the Lord's Supper, the two ordinances flowing from the pierced side. The text does not say this, and the link is an application and not an exegetical claim.

debates.bearing: The first two readings are not rivals. A real death is the basis of real cleansing and the gift of the Spirit, and the sacramental reading is acceptable only as an application of those truths.

debates.question: Who is the one who 'handed Me over' in verse 11?

views.label: Caiaphas and the leaders
views.case: John 18:30 and 35 say the chief priests handed Jesus over to Pilate. Caiaphas, who has already planned His death, 11:49 to 52, stands at the head of that action, and it fits 'greater sin' because he knew the Scriptures and still delivered the Messiah.

views.label: Judas
views.case: Judas is the one who handed Him over to the arresting party in 18:2 and 5. John uses this verb for Judas consistently, which suggests that the 'greater sin' may be the betrayal by one of His own.

views.label: The whole chain of those who delivered Him
views.case: Others argue that Jesus is speaking generally, of all in the chain from Judas to the priests, as a contrast with Pilate, whose authority is given from above. Pilate's sin is less because he acted in ignorance of who Jesus is.

debates.bearing: On every reading, Pilate's authority is derived and God's purpose is above it, as Jesus says. That does not excuse Pilate, but it changes the question of who is in charge.

study.originalLanguages:
The most famous word of the chapter is the single Greek word of verse 30, tetelestai, 'It is finished.' It is the perfect tense of teleo, to bring to an end, to complete, to accomplish. The perfect marks a completed action whose results continue. John has prepared for it carefully. In 4:34 Jesus says His food is to do the will of the one who sent Him and to finish His work, and in 5:36 the works the Father has given Him to accomplish testify about Him. In 17:4 He says He has completed the work, using a related verb, teleioo. Verse 28 uses teleo for the whole scene: knowing that everything 'had now been accomplished,' He speaks the word that fulfils Scripture. The cry is therefore not a sigh of relief at the end of suffering but an announcement that the Father's work has been done. It is about work and not simply about pain.

The next phrase, paredoken to pneuma, is usually translated 'He yielded up His spirit.' The verb is the one for handing over, which the Gospel has used all through the trial for the handing over of Jesus by Judas, by the priests and by Pilate, 18:30 and 35 and 19:16. Now it is Jesus who hands over. He does so freely, and the literal sense, 'handed over the spirit,' is open to a second hearing. In 20:22 the risen Lord breathes on the disciples and says 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' John may be inviting the reader to hear both: He gives up His life, and the gift of the Spirit is made possible by His death. The phrase 'bowing His head' is also unusual. The verb klino, to incline or lay down, is the one Jesus used in Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58 of having nowhere to lay His head. Here, at the end, He has one place to lay it, and He does so Himself, before He dies, as though in control of the moment.

The soldier 'pierced' His side with a spear in verse 34, and verse 37 quotes the Hebrew prophet that they will look on the one they have pierced. John's verb in verse 34 is nysso, a word for stabbing or pricking, and the quotation in verse 37 uses a different verb from the Greek of that period, ekkenteo, which means to pierce through. The two verbs describe the same event and one prophecy, and John asks us to see them together. The word 'testified' in verse 35 is perfect, memartyreken, and describes testimony that stands on record, which fits the insistence that the witness is true.

The word for the notice on the cross is titlos, a Latin loan word that John uses in the Greek form, as he does for the Praetorium and for the Latin title. In verse 22, Pilate's answer 'What I have written, I have written' uses the perfect, gegrapha, 'it stands written.' The perfect tense is the one regularly used in the Gospel when Scripture is cited, as 'it is written,' and John may be inviting the reader to hear in the governor's refusal to change the text something like the authority of Scripture. The title is fixed, and it is true.

The word for authority in verse 11 is exousia, and Jesus says it was given to Pilate 'from above,' anothen. The same adverb stands in 3:3 and 3:7, where it means both 'again' and 'from above,' and in 3:31, where the one who comes 'from above' is above all. In the trial it fixes the direction of authority: it comes down from God and is delegated, and it will be called to account. And finally, the question 'Where are You from?' in verse 9, pothen ei su, is the question of origin that the whole Gospel has been asking, as in 7:27 and 9:29. Pilate has no idea that he has asked it, and Jesus does not answer because the answer has been given in 18:36 and 37.

typology.fulfillment: The Passover lamb was killed on the afternoon of the Preparation, its blood marked the doorposts with hyssop, Exodus 12:22, and none of its bones could be broken, Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12. In John, Jesus is crucified at the time the lambs are being made ready, the sponge is lifted on a hyssop stalk, and His bones are left unbroken, verses 29, 33 and 36. John the Baptist's greeting, 'the Lamb of God,' 1:29, is the key. The escalation is that the blood of this Lamb does not only spare households from judgment but takes away the sin of the world, and Paul says Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The type falls short because one lamb was killed for each household and the deliverance was from Egypt; here one Lamb dies for people from every nation and the deliverance is from sin and death.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer of Psalm 22, John 19:23-24
typology.fulfillment: In Psalm 22, a righteous man surrounded by enemies cries to God and sees them divide his garments and cast lots for his clothing, Psalm 22:18. The correspondence in John is exact, since the soldiers do this, and John shows that even the seamless tunic and the casting of lots fit what was written. The escalation is that David's experience is a pattern that comes to its full meaning in the one who is both David's Son and David's Lord. The psalm, which begins in desolation, ends with praise that reaches the nations, Psalm 22:27 to 31, and this is where the Gospel is leading. The type falls short because David's suffering was a partial, personal experience, and the cross is the final, representative one.

Zechariah has the LORD pouring out a spirit of grace and prayer on Jerusalem so that they look on the One they pierced and mourn. John 19:37 cites it and Revelation 1:7 repeats it of the return. The correspondence is of the pierced one who is looked on and mourned. The escalation is that Zechariah's pierced one speaks in the first person of the LORD, so the one pierced is God Himself, and John presents Jesus as that person. The prophecy then goes on to the fountain for cleansing, Zechariah 13:1, which John's mention of blood and water recalls. The type falls short because in Zechariah the mourning is a promise yet to come, and in John the piercing is by a soldier who does not know what he does, while the mourning and the cleansing belong to those who respond in faith.

typology.type: The garden and the new tomb, John 19:41
typology.fulfillment: The garden, in John 18:1 and 19:41 and 20:15, recalls the first garden, where life began and was lost, Genesis 2 and 3. The tomb is new, a place where no one had been laid, so that when the body is gone nobody can say it was someone else's. The correspondence is of a garden where a man is placed and a story turns. The escalation is that the first Adam fell asleep in a garden and a bride was taken from his side, Genesis 2:21 and 22, while from the last Adam's pierced side blood and water flow, and from His death a new people is born. This second parallel is an application and not a claim the text makes, and it should be held lightly. The type falls short because Eden was a place of innocence which was lost, while this garden is the place where the first fruits of new creation are about to rise.

study.christ:
The cross is here presented as the throne of the true king. Pilate sets Jesus before the people and says 'Here is the man,' verse 5, and 'Here is your King,' verse 14, without knowing that both are accurate. The crown of thorns, the purple robe and the title on the cross are all given as insults, but each states what is true. John did not need to explain the irony; he only needed to report it. Jesus is the king of a kingdom not of this world, and He is crowned in the way that kingdom is established, by giving Himself for His people. The prophet Isaiah had said that the Servant would be 'disfigured beyond that of any man,' Isaiah 52:14, and would offer His back to those who struck Him, Isaiah 50:6, and then be 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' Isaiah 52:13. John joins these: the lifting up is both the cross and the exaltation, 12:32.

He is also the Lamb. Everything in verses 28 to 37 points back to the Passover and to the words of John the Baptist in 1:29. The time is the Preparation. The hyssop recalls the doorposts. The unbroken bones fit the regulation for the lamb. And the blood and water from the side tell us that this death is both a sacrifice and the source of life. Hebrews says He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, Hebrews 9:12.

The cry 'It is finished' is the climax of the whole Gospel. The one who said He had come to finish the Father's work, 4:34, now announces that it is done. Believers can rest on it for their acceptance with God, as Paul says Christ canceled the debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. And Jesus is in control to the end. He knows that all is accomplished, He speaks of His thirst so that Scripture is fulfilled, He bows His head, and He gives up His spirit. This does not mean He did not suffer. His thirst is real and His death is real, which is why the soldier's spear finds Him dead. It means the death was the Son's own act, as He had said in 10:17 and 18.

A word of care is needed. The seamless tunic is sometimes taken as a picture of the unity of the church or of the high priest's robe, and the link with Mary and the beloved disciple is sometimes taken as the founding of a particular doctrine. John does not draw those lines, and they are best treated as suggestions, not as what the text says. What the text says is firm enough. Jesus provides for His mother, completes the work, gives up His spirit, is pierced and is buried in a garden by two men who come out into the open. The Christ of John 19 is the King, the Lamb and the Son who gives Himself, and that is enough.
study.god:
The chapter's picture of God is one of sovereign purpose through human sin. Pilate is the most powerful man in the room, and he is afraid. 'Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?' he says, and Jesus answers that he would have none 'if it were not given to you from above,' verse 11. The same God who gives governors their authority, as Paul says in Romans 13:1, is the one carrying out His plan through them. Peter says the same on Pentecost: Jesus was delivered up 'by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and by the hands of the lawless they killed Him, Acts 2:23. Both are true at once. Human sin is real, and the sinners are guilty, so Jesus says the one who handed Him over has the greater sin. God's plan is complete, and no one outside His rule is able to thwart it.

The chapter also shows a God who keeps His word. Four times in the account of the cross John notes that Scripture was fulfilled. Each time he cites a text from a different part of the Old Testament, the Psalms, the Law and the prophets. The scene is not improvised. The God who spoke to David about the division of his garments, who gave Moses the Passover regulations, and who spoke through Zechariah about the pierced one, is the God who has now brought it all together. His faithfulness is shown in the smallest details, which is why believers can rely on His promises that have not yet come to pass.

Here too the character of God's justice and mercy meet. The cross is the place where sin is condemned and where sinners are saved. Paul says that God showed His righteousness in the cross, so that He might be just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25 and 26. The blood and water from the side tell us that the judgment poured out on the Son is also the source of cleansing, which is what Zechariah promised. The God who is holy enough to demand atonement is loving enough to provide it, and He does so by giving the Son.

Finally, the chapter shows the God who is present in suffering. John does not include the cry of abandonment found in Matthew and Mark, but he does show the Son in complete obedience to the Father to the end, and he shows a God who is not distant from human pain. The Son thirsts, is mocked and dies, and in doing so shows the Father's heart, as Jesus says in 14:9, whoever has seen Him has seen the Father. Worship therefore takes the shape of wonder. The glory of God is seen in the lifting up of the Son on a cross, and there is no place of human shame or loss to which He has not gone.

crossReferences.note: 'They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.' John quotes this at 19:24 and shows the soldiers doing it, with a detail about the seamless tunic that makes the lot necessary. The whole psalm, which begins with abandonment and ends with the nations worshiping, stands behind the scene.

The righteous sufferer says that in his thirst he was given vinegar. This is one of the passages John has in mind when he says Jesus spoke of His thirst 'to fulfill the Scripture,' 19:28. Psalm 69:4 is cited elsewhere in the Gospel for the hatred that had no reason, 15:25.

Of the Passover lamb: 'you may not break any of the bones.' John 19:36 cites a regulation of this kind, and Numbers 9:12 repeats it. The soldiers' decision not to break Jesus' legs places Him in the role of the lamb at the moment of its death.

At the first Passover a cluster of hyssop was dipped in the blood and brushed on the doorframe. John mentions that the sour wine was lifted to Jesus on a hyssop stalk, 19:29, a small detail that points to the Passover setting without being explained.

The LORD says 'they will look on Me, the One they have pierced,' and mourning follows. John 19:37 cites it at the spear thrust, and Revelation 1:7 uses it of the return. It identifies the pierced Jesus with the God of the prophecy.

A body hung on a tree is under God's curse and must be buried the same day. This explains the leaders' concern about the bodies and the burial before the Sabbath. Paul takes it further in Galatians 3:13, where Christ becomes a curse for us.

The Servant was assigned a grave with the wicked and was with a rich man in His death. Joseph of Arimathea's tomb and Nicodemus's spices fit this. John does not cite the verse, but the new tomb of a wealthy disciple makes the link close.

John the Baptist's first public word about Jesus is 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' The Gospel opens with the title and closes its account of the death with the lamb's bones, and the whole book is held between the two.

'No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord.' The control Jesus shows at the cross, in the thirst, the declaration and the bowing of His head, is the content of this promise made earlier in the Gospel.

'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' Paul states plainly what John arranges in detail. The earliest Christians understood the cross in Passover terms from the start, and John's timing and symbols are in line with that.

Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify the people by His own blood. The place of the skull outside the walls, John 19:17 and 20, is given a meaning: He went outside so that His people might be brought in.

The Spirit, the water and the blood testify together. The letter written by the same tradition ties the water and blood to the truth that Jesus came in the flesh and gave life, and it echoes the witness of John 19:34 and 35.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a man made from the ground who is told that disobedience will bring death, and with a serpent whose head is promised to be crushed, Genesis 3:15. The long story that follows is a search for how that death can be undone and the curse lifted. The Law gives the sacrifices, the Passover gives the lamb, the Psalms give the voice of the righteous sufferer, and the prophets give the pierced one and the Servant who bears sin. John 19 is where these roads meet. Everything that the Old Testament has been saying for centuries about substitution, kingship, sacrifice and suffering is collected in one afternoon outside Jerusalem.

In the garden of Eden the curse came on the ground and the man was told he would return to dust. On the cross the one who is without sin comes under the curse of being hung on a tree, Galatians 3:13. At the first Passover a lamb died so that the firstborn could live. Here the Lamb of God dies so that the world can live. In Israel's long history the king was meant to reign for his people, and one after another failed. Here the true king takes the throne by giving Himself. Where the first couple reached for a tree and found shame and death, the last Adam takes a tree and by it breaks death.

The account also answers the problem of the divided people. The soldiers divide the clothes, but the seamless tunic is not torn, and the beloved disciple takes Jesus' mother as his own. A new family is formed at the foot of the cross, which is how John prepares for the church. Joseph and Nicodemus, one of whom is a secret disciple and the other a night visitor, come out into the light. The people who are gathered by the death of Jesus are those who were afraid and those who were far, and they stand together by a tomb.

The story goes on from here. The garden tomb is the place where the first day of the new week begins, and Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord and takes him for the gardener, 20:15. The pierced one reappears in the book of Revelation as a Lamb standing as though slain, in the middle of the throne, Revelation 5:6, and as the one whom every eye will see, Revelation 1:7. The water that flowed from His side is answered by the river of the water of life in the last chapter of the Bible, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1. In the new creation there is no more curse, Revelation 22:3, because the one who bore it has finished what He came to do.

quiz.q: How does John present Jesus' kingship at the crucifixion?

options.text: Even the mockery and the trilingual sign unwittingly proclaim the truth that Jesus is King.
options.note: The recurring title and the inscription state the truth through irony; He reigns from the cross.

options.text: Jesus finally abandons any claim to be a king.
options.note: The chapter presents Him as King throughout, even in the inscription Pilate refuses to change.

options.text: The kingship is merely a joke with no deeper meaning.
options.note: The soldiers mean it as mockery, but John shows it states the truth of His reign.

options.text: He is crowned and robed as a king in mockery.
options.note: True, but it misses John's irony that the mock kingship proclaims His real royalty.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' cry It is finished mean?

options.text: The saving work the Father gave Him is complete, a shout of accomplishment, not defeat.
options.note: The single word tetelestai declares the atonement finished and the Scriptures fulfilled.

options.text: He had endured all He could bear.
options.note: He did not merely run out of strength; He deliberately yielded up His spirit once the work was accomplished.

options.text: He was giving up on His mission.
options.note: The opposite; the mission is accomplished, not abandoned.

options.text: His suffering was at last over.
options.note: His suffering did end, but the cry means the saving work itself is completed, not merely that pain stopped.

quiz.q: Why does John stress that Jesus' bones were not broken?

options.text: To show He is the true Passover Lamb, whose bones must not be broken.
options.note: Verse 36 cites the Passover Scripture; Jesus fulfills the lamb typology.

options.text: Because it was a lucky coincidence.
options.note: John presents it as the deliberate fulfillment of Scripture, not chance.

options.text: Because He was already dead, so breaking them was not needed.
options.note: That is why they did not break them, but John's point is the fulfillment of the Passover Scripture that no bone would be broken.

options.text: To show Scripture was being fulfilled.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific Passover Lamb typology the detail proclaims.

quiz.q: What did Jesus do for His mother from the cross?

options.text: He entrusted her to the care of the beloved disciple.
options.note: Verses 26 and 27 show His tender provision for His mother even while dying.

options.text: He arranged for others to look after her later.
options.note: He did provide for her care, but by entrusting her then and there to the beloved disciple as his own mother.

options.text: He ignored her in His suffering.
options.note: He deliberately cared for her amid His agony.

options.text: He commended her to a disciple's household.
options.note: True, but it slightly understates the tenderness of Woman, here is your son, and here is your mother.

quiz.q: How is Jesus buried, according to the chapter?

options.text: Joseph and Nicodemus wrap Him with abundant spices and lay Him in a new garden tomb.
options.note: Verses 38 to 42 describe the honorable burial in a new tomb.

options.text: He is left unburied on the cross.
options.note: He is taken down and buried with care by Joseph and Nicodemus.

options.text: He is buried hastily with no special care.
options.note: He was buried in haste before the Sabbath, but with lavish spices in a new garden tomb, an honorable burial.

options.text: Two secret disciples give Him a proper burial.
options.note: True, but it omits the detail of the new garden tomb and the abundant spices, marking an honorable, even royal, burial.

questions: The King of the world reigned from a cross, crowned with thorns. How does this upside-down kingship reshape your idea of power and greatness?
Jesus reminded Pilate that his authority was given from above. How does it steady you to know God is sovereign even over those who seem to hold power over you?
It is finished was a cry of completion. What are you tempted to add to Christ's finished work to feel accepted, and how does His cry free you?
Jesus is the true Passover Lamb whose blood shields His people. How does knowing your deliverance was bought at such cost move your gratitude?
Even in agony Jesus cared for His mother. How does His attentiveness to one person in the midst of His suffering encourage you to trust His care for you?

translationNotes.note: The day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour; the BSB footnote gives about noon. Jesus is condemned as the Passover lambs are being prepared, underscoring the Lamb typology.
The sour wine was lifted on a stalk of hyssop, the plant used to apply the Passover blood in Exodus 12:22, a deliberate echo, and fulfilling Psalm 69:21.
It is finished renders the single Greek word tetelestai, a shout of completion used for a debt paid in full; the saving work is accomplished.
Not one of His bones will be broken cites Psalm 34:20 and the Passover law of Exodus 12:46; They will look on the One they have pierced cites Zechariah 12:10.
